baselineDisplay.title: The coming energy crisis
baselineDisplay.text:
More than two hundred years ago, the world experienced an energy revolution that launched the Industrial Age. Ever since then, with the rapid increase in population density, the industrialized world’s thirst for energy has more than tripled. Petroleum and natural gas are exploited as versatile and high-quality energy products. Uranium is also tapped to fuel nuclear reactors and provide atomic energy.
Cheap energy is the lifeblood of human society. But there is a dark side to the near monopoly of non-renewable fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas, along with the controversial uranium, to supply our growing energy demand. The availability of these fuels is physically limited, and their use threatens our health and environment. Multiple international treaties have been proposed to limit the use of fossil fuels for this very reason. Fears of global warming aside, burning fossil fuels releases chemicals and particulates that can cause breathing problems, cancer as well as brain and nerve damage. Nuclear energy, once hailed as “too cheap to meter”, hasn’t been highly economically successful when all costs are factored in. Furthermore, public opinion polls show nuclear energy is too closely associated with disasters like the Chernobyl reactor meltdown and the Fukushima explosion, and with the danger that rebel insurgents could do damage with the toxic waste. Inexpensive and seemingly abundant non-renewable energy from dead plants and extinct animals fueled the 20th-century economy, but geologists, climatologists, environmentalists, and many others are warning that the honeymoon may soon be over.
At some indefinite time in the near future, the last drop of oil, lump of coal, or wisp of natural gas will be collected from the earth. The eventual depletion of fossil fuels that hitherto proved so reliable has left us with no choice but to prepare for a new age of energy synthesis. Most certainly, human demand for energy will not decrease or plateau but surge as the world population grows to nine billion before 2040. It is no surprise that world energy consumption is projected to show a linear increase of 50 percent in the future.
How will we meet the skyrocketing energy demand of the future? Until we perfect the technology of cold fusion, we’ll have to focus on the development and increased production of energy from renewable energy sources – sun, wind, water, and so on. While renewable energy sources are promising, an international confederation of scientists and engineers is working feverishly to overcome the various obstacles associated with these “new energy” technologies. The major challenge is to develop efficient and economically workable versions of these technologies.
Take solar energy, for example. It is a good option because there is an unlimited supply of glittering sunlight. Making it work on a large scale, however, is much easier said than done. It would be cost-prohibitive to take the intricate gadgets of solar energy from the fringe of “green” society to the mainstream for major world consumption. The solar apparatus itself is ready for many new business and consumer applications, but it is way too expensive to replace the old combustion machinery of gears and motors with new electronic technology of semiconductors and transistors on a global or even a national scale.
Wind power, which has been used effectively in some places for generations, is also rapidly growing in the energy market. The principle behind it is that wind converts rotary force into electricity by turning the blades of the turbine clockwise or counterclockwise around an axis. Unfortunately, wind power is very unreliable and its strength depends on local weather patterns, temperature, time of year, and location. In addition to this unreliability, wind power equipment is very expensive compared with other energy sources and won’t become a viable alternative until we can slash the costs significantly. Also, a wind farm requires enormous land clearing to produce significant amounts of energy.
Hydroelectric power is another source of clean and renewable energy. It can be harnessed by controlling the natural outflow of water with different methods. The most popular is through dams, which, unfortunately, can have negative environmental impacts if not designed with careful forethought. Most of the hydroelectric dams in the world are historically recent, but all reservoirs need to be maintained on a regular basis. Otherwise, they can eventually fill up with mud and have to be cleared up through very expensive excavation to become useful again.
Biomass energy derived from plant and animal matter is still another renewable source being considered as a standby replacement for fossil fuels. Organic waste in the form of dead trees, leaves, animal corpses and food processing waste exists in abundance and can be used to produce energy. However, there is no way to ventilate the direct burning of biomass as fuel without diffusing carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. These gases can pose a risk to the ozone layer, increasing the overall exposure of human beings to harmful UV rays from the sun. Besides, it takes time and money to collect biomass and transport it in its raw form to a central point for processing into fuel, and the automation of such a process is too difficult. So, for the time being, biomass has too many costly drawbacks to be a workable alternative to fossil fuels.
Although renewable energies are not yet economically competitive with fossil fuels, their prices become more attractive when compared with the health and environmental costs associated with burning coal and oil. Perhaps the best solution to our growing energy challenges comes in a bulletin from the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS): “Our society’s future success cannot hinge on one single solution. The answer instead must come from a family of diverse energy technologies that share a unified purpose -- they do not deplete our natural resources or destroy our environment.” Despite the difficulties, it is important to remember that an energy crisis is approaching at a supersonic speed and will soon be upon us. In order to inaugurate a new era of energy, we must act quickly and work toward international collaboration to find the most effective solutions to our energy problem.

corrections.before: Until we perfect the technology of cold fusion,
corrections.after: While scientists continue to investigate nuclear fusion as a potential energy source,
corrections.evidence: 冷聚变未得到可重复的D-D证实，不能描述为已成立而只需完善的能源技术。

corrections.before: Also, a wind farm requires enormous land clearing to produce significant amounts of energy.
corrections.after: Also, a wind farm may occupy a large area, although much of the land between turbines can remain in agricultural use.
corrections.evidence: DOE区分风场总范围与实际设施占地，不能说必然全面清地。

corrections.before: These gases can pose a risk to the ozone layer, increasing the overall exposure of human beings to harmful UV rays from the sun.
corrections.after: These gases can contribute to global warming by trapping heat in the atmosphere.
corrections.evidence: 修正温室效应与臭氧损耗混淆，EPA气候科学可互证。

notes: 9段全文及PDF164–166通读复核。保留作者能源危机预测、当时成本观点与九十亿人口预测，不把原作改写为2026市场报告；修正冷聚变成熟度暗示、风场全面清地误解及CO2导致臭氧损耗的科学错误。第4及8段跨页均完整，修订后复读。
